Overheard

When you travel, stations and airports are full of announcements, signs and screens, often in a language you don't speak. Overheard knows your bookings and tells you only the ones that affect you, in your language, with proof.

30-second wrap

"We tested it on 74 examples. Gemini caught 18 of 18 practice announcements that mattered, and all 3 real news stories that mattered. Its weak spot is the one you saw: flight numbers that differ by one digit. Next, I want a phone app that listens in the background, with big-text modes for older riders. All the code and test results are on GitHub, including the failures."

Model lines: say these while things load

One sentence each. Good for the rehearse and photo waits, or when a judge asks which models you used.

  • Short version: "Each Gemini model has one job: one decides, one reads, one writes and translates, one double-checks, one speaks, and one draws the proof."
  • Decision model (gemini-decision-1): "This is the one that decides. It answers all 286 yes/no questions about my trip at the same time, in under a second."
  • Neon: "Neon reads my booking emails and turns them into a trip plan. When something does affect me, Neon says what changed and what I should do."
  • Hydrogen: "Hydrogen writes the yes/no questions in French, Dutch and English, and translates every alert into my language."
  • Hydrogen with Google Search: "Hydrogen also searches local news for strikes and closures on my dates. Then my code opens every link and checks every date."
  • Carbon: "When the decision model isn't sure, Carbon takes a second look. In our tests it caught all 3 practice items the first model missed."
  • Text to speech: "Gemini's voice model reads the alert out loud in my language."
  • Nano Banana: "Nano Banana circles the right line on my own photo, so I can see the proof."
  • Managed Agent: "For video, a Gemini agent cuts out the few seconds that matter, using ffmpeg on Google's servers."
  • Gemini CLI: "Gemini also helped me build it. It wrote the 6 sample booking emails in 20 seconds and all 36 practice announcements in under a minute."
  • Speed: "The decision model took under a second each time. Asking a regular chat model took 4 to 7 seconds."
20 seconds

The pitch and why I built it

Train stations and airports talk at you all day, often in a language you don't speak, and almost none of it is about you. Overheard knows your bookings. It listens to announcements and reads signs and local news. It only speaks up when something affects your trip, in your language, and it shows you the proof.

Why, in my words

"My friends call me their tour guide, in New York and wherever we travel. Still, when I travel alone I worry about missing an announcement or taking a wrong turn. On the subway I see older people and people who are new to English struggle when an announcement is hard to hear or plans change at the last minute. Overheard knows your trip and tells you only what matters."

Words used on this page

Four words to know

BookingOne thing you reserved: a flight, a hotel, a train, a museum ticket. The demo trip has 6.
Question listAbout 286 yes/no questions Gemini writes about your bookings, like "Is this about Eurostar 9315?". The code calls it a fingerprint.
Look-alikeAn announcement that sounds like yours but isn't, like a different train number. The tests mix these in on purpose.
ReceiptA short note for each thing Overheard heard and ignored, with its score, so you can see why it stayed quiet.
What it looks like

The phone screens

How it works

Five steps

  1. Read the bookings. Gemini reads your booking emails (read-only Gmail access) and makes a trip plan.
  2. Write the questions. Gemini writes about 40 to 54 yes/no questions for each booking, in French, Dutch and English.
  3. Check everything it hears or sees. Each announcement, photo or news story goes to Gemini's decision model, which answers every question at once and gives each booking a score from 0 to 1.
  4. Decide. 0.8 or higher: it alerts you. Between 0.4 and 0.8: a second model, Carbon, takes a look. Below 0.4: it stays quiet and writes a receipt.
  5. Tell you, with proof. It translates the alert and reads it out loud. Then it shows the sentence it heard, or your photo with the line circled.

Extra features

  • News check before you fly. Gemini searches French and Dutch news for strikes and closures on your dates. The code opens every link and checks every date.
  • Practice mode. Plays announcements you are likely to hear on your trip, some about you and some look-alikes, so you can see how it reacts.
  • "Not about me" button. When it gets one wrong, you tap this. Gemini writes up to 3 new questions for that booking and keeps them only if they don't block real alerts.

How Gemini helped build it

  • Gemini CLI with Hydrogen wrote the 6 sample booking emails in 20 seconds.
  • It wrote all 36 practice announcements, with the right answers, in 56 seconds. None needed fixing.
  • Gemini CLI with Carbon double-checked the labels on all 38 news stories and agreed with every one.

I built the New York subway version first, in the afternoon. Then I split the travel version into 8 parts and ran them at the same time in separate Claude Code sessions, with Gemini CLI doing the jobs above. 71 automated tests pass, and every Gemini call is logged with its time.

Does it work?

Results and failures

We tested 74 examples against the 6-booking trip: 36 practice announcements and signs (half about the trip, half look-alikes) and 38 real news stories found on the day.

TestMethodCaughtFalse alarmsTime
Practice announcements
12 about me, 12 look-alikes		Decision model alone10 of 122 of 120.93 s
With Carbon for unsure ones12 of 122 of 122.6 s
Write it out, then ask a chat model12 of 120 of 126.5 s
Practice signs
6 about me, 6 look-alikes		Decision model alone5 of 60 of 60.56 s
With Carbon for unsure ones6 of 61 of 62.3 s
Real news
3 about me, 35 not		Decision model alone3 of 35 of 350.73 s
Ask a chat model3 of 37 of 354.1 s
Simple keyword search2 of 311 of 35n/a

What the numbers mean

  • The decision model is the fast one. Writing everything out and asking a chat model was more accurate on practice data, but 7 to 12 times slower.
  • Carbon helps catch misses. It caught all 3 practice items the first model missed, and added 2 false alarms.
  • "Not about me" works in testing. One tap took a real New York subway false alarm from 0.79 to 0.01, and the real alert stayed at 0.92.
  • Blurry photos are where it shines. On the subway tests, with blurry signs, it still caught 7 of 8. Reading the text first caught only 4 of 8.

What went wrong

  • close call A Paris metro closure alerted on the train booking (0.845) when it should have gone to the hotel (0.843).
  • one-digit mix-up "KL 643 gate change, KL 641 on time" alerted every time. One tap on "Not about me" fixes it on the tests.
  • small test Only 3 real news stories mattered, so that result rests on very few examples.
  • speed The decision takes about 1 s. The translated alert takes about 10 s, the voice about 18 s and the circled photo 25 to 35 s.
  • made-up audio The practice announcements were generated by Gemini, so they are cleaner than a real noisy platform.
Next

What comes next

  • A phone app that listens in the background. Today you tap to listen.
  • Ask out loud. "Which platform now?" and hear the answer while you walk, using Gemini's live voice.
  • More countries and languages. Mostly a matter of adding local news sources and practice data.
  • Learning from other travellers. One person's "Not about me" could help everyone on the same train.
  • Easier for older and low-vision riders. Bigger text and slower speech, with the photo described out loud.
Judge questions

Likely questions, simple answers

Why not just use Google Translate?

Translate turns every announcement into words, and you still have to read them all and work out which ones matter. Overheard does that part for you and stays quiet otherwise.

Why not TripIt or the airline app?

Those know your bookings, but they can't hear the station speaker or read a paper sign taped to a pillar. Overheard checks those too, with one engine.

Why use the decision model instead of a chat model?

It's much faster: under a second, against 4 to 7 seconds. It gives a yes/no score for every question, which makes it easy to set a cut-off. A chat model was a bit more accurate on practice data, so unsure cases go to Carbon.

How do you stop false alarms?

It only alerts if the announcement matches your booking and also describes a change. Scores between 0.4 and 0.8 get a second look from Carbon. News outside your travel dates is ignored. On real news the decision model raised 5 false alarms out of 35, and all 5 were close calls.

How fast is it?

The decision takes about 1 second. The translated alert arrives in about 10 seconds, the voice in about 18, and the circled photo in 25 to 35. Shrinking the audio and photos first cut the decision from 3.4 seconds to 0.8.

Is my email safe?

It only asks for read-only access. The demo uses a test inbox with 6 sample bookings, and the login keys stay on my laptop. The email text is sent to Gemini to read the bookings.

What's real and what's made up?

Real: the 38 news stories found today, the live New York subway alerts, real station noise and 4 real signs in the subway tests, and the Gmail connection. Made up: the practice announcements and signs (generated by Gemini) and the 6 bookings.

What broke?

A close call sent a Paris metro closure to the train instead of the hotel. Flight numbers that differ by one digit still fool it. The first version of "Not about me" blocked real alerts too, until I fixed it. One Gemini call once froze for 3 minutes, so it now gives up after 30 seconds and tries another model.

You tapped "Not about me". Why not play the clip again?

Because in practice it still fired. That clip also mentions a real gate change, so the new questions didn't match it. In the tests, one tap took a real false alarm from 0.79 to 0.01.

How did one person build this in a day?

I built the New York subway version first. Then I split the travel version into 8 parts and ran them at the same time in separate coding sessions. Gemini CLI wrote the sample emails and practice announcements and double-checked the news labels. 71 tests pass.

Where is the AI agent used?

For video. Each second of video is checked like a photo, and a Gemini agent cuts out the important seconds with ffmpeg on Google's servers. It takes about 66 seconds.

Does the mic stay on all the time?

Not yet. You tap to listen. Always-on listening needs a proper phone app, which is the first next step.

What does it cost to run?

I haven't measured the cost per trip yet. The decision model runs on every input and is the cheapest step. The expensive steps only run when something affects you.

What's next?

A phone app, asking questions out loud, more countries, learning from other travellers, and modes for older and low-vision riders.
